2. WHAT “ALL-ON-X” MEANS, AND WHAT IT DOES NOT MEAN
•
The “X” is not fixed. It is the number of implants needed to support the bridge. The final number, position and angle are decided during surgery,
once your surgeon can see and feel the bone. Fewer or more implants than planned may be placed.
•
Same-day teeth are temporary teeth. If your implants are stable enough on the day of surgery, a temporary fixed bridge is attached. It is made
of acrylic or printed resin, it is not the final result, and it is expected to chip, stain, wear or break during the months of healing. The final bridge is
made later and will look and feel different.
•
This is a prosthesis, not a set of new natural teeth. The bridge is a device that is screwed onto implants. It does not feel, chew or age like
natural teeth. It requires daily cleaning under the bridge, professional maintenance, and eventual repair and replacement.
•
What is removed cannot be put back. Extraction of the remaining teeth and reduction of the jaw bone are permanent. If this treatment fails, the
options remaining to me may be fewer and more difficult than the ones I have today, and a conventional denture on a reduced ridge may fit
poorly.
Longevity, in plain numbers. Implants often last a long time; the bridge on top of them does not last as long. In published follow-up studies of
full-arch fixed prostheses, essentially every prosthesis needed at least one repair by about six years, and roughly 4 out of 5 prostheses were
still in service at 5 years and about 3 out of 5 at 10 years. These figures come from studies of other patients and are not a promise about my
own result. Replacement of a worn or fractured bridge is additional treatment at additional cost.

Patient: ______________________________
3. RISKS OF THE SURGERY
No surgery is risk-free, and no result can be promised or guaranteed. This list cannot include every possible complication.
•
Common, and usually temporary: considerable pain, swelling and bruising of the face and neck for several days — usually more than after a
simple extraction; bleeding and oozing for the first day; stiff jaw and limited mouth opening; sore throat; cracked corners of the mouth; bruising
that can track down the neck and chest; difficulty eating for weeks.
•
Less common: infection needing antibiotics, drainage or a second procedure; wound opening and slow healing; damage to the lips, cheeks,
tongue or corners of the mouth; jaw joint (TMJ) pain, clicking or locking; hematoma; scarring; small pieces of bone that work their way out later;
allergic or other adverse reaction to a medicine or material.
•
Uncommon, but serious: nerve injury — numbness, tingling, burning or pain of the lower lip, chin, gums or tongue, and/or a change or loss of
taste. The lower jaw carries the higher risk, and bone reduction brings the surgery closer to the nerve. This usually improves over weeks to
months, but it can last longer and in some cases is permanent; an opening between the mouth and the sinus or nose; fracture of a thin, atrophic
lower jaw, which may require hospital treatment and plating; infection spreading into the face or neck; heavy bleeding.
•
Rare: medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw (MRONJ) — bone that will not heal and stays exposed; the risk is higher with
bone-strengthening or anti-cancer drugs (alendronate, zoledronic acid, denosumab and similar) or previous radiation to the jaws; permanent
change in facial appearance; life-threatening complications.
If zygomatic, pterygoid or trans-sinus implants are used, these additional risks apply:
•
sinus infection or long-term sinusitis, sometimes needing ENT treatment or removal of the implant; oro-antral communication; nasal congestion
or discharge;
•
injury to the infraorbital nerve causing numbness of the cheek, side of the nose or upper lip;
•
penetration into the orbit (eye socket) or, very rarely, injury to the eye or its contents; bruising around the eye; temporary double vision;
•
these implants are technically difficult to remove if they fail, and removal is a larger operation.
4. RISKS SPECIFIC TO FULL-ARCH IMPLANT TREATMENT
•
Not enough stability on the day. If the implants are not firm enough to carry a bridge immediately, same-day fixed teeth will not be
delivered. I will wear a removable temporary denture, which sits on the healing gums and is often uncomfortable, for several months.
•
Implant failure. One or more implants can fail to fuse with the bone, or can fail later. Depending on which implant and when, this may mean
additional surgery, additional implants, grafting, a remake of the bridge, a return to a removable denture, or — if enough implants fail — loss of
the whole plan.
•
Bone reduction is permanent. Reshaping the ridge lowers it and changes its form. A denture made before surgery will not fit afterwards, and a
conventional denture on a reduced ridge is usually less stable than it was before.
•
Speech and adaptation. Most people develop a lisp or altered speech at first and adapt over weeks. Some do not fully adapt. Air or saliva may
escape at the sides. The bulk of the bridge and its position may change how I sound.
•
Cleaning and food trapping. There is a space under the bridge, and food and air pass under it. Cleaning requires a water flosser, superfloss or
threaders, every day, for life. The bridge must be unscrewed and professionally cleaned periodically, which is a separate appointment and fee.
•
Gum and bone changes. Peri-implant mucositis and peri-implantitis (inflammation with bone loss) can develop around the implants. Gums
shrink over time, which may expose the metal, the junction between the bridge and the gum, or dark spaces — a particular concern if I have a
high smile line. This junction may be visible when I smile or speak.
•
Prosthesis and hardware problems. Chipping and wear of the teeth; fracture of the bridge or its framework; loosening or fracture of screws
and abutments; staining of the access holes; a screw or fragment that is difficult to retrieve. Grinding and clenching (bruxism) sharply
increases all of these, and a protective night guard is usually required — and is my responsibility to wear.
•
Bite, joint and opposing arch. The bite and the vertical height of my face may be changed on purpose. This can affect the jaw joints and
muscles. A hard bridge chewing against natural teeth or another prosthesis can wear or damage the opposing arch, which may then also need
treatment.
•
Appearance. The shape, size, color and lip support of the final bridge are limited by the position of my implants, the bone and the space
available. The result may not match the appearance I imagined, and there are limits to how much it can be changed once the implants are
placed.
•
Systemic and habit factors. Smoking or vaping, uncontrolled diabetes, bruxism, steroids or drugs that lower immunity, previous radiation, and
poor hygiene all significantly increase the chance of infection, bone loss and failure of this treatment.
•
Imaging. Implants and frameworks cause scatter on CT and MRI images. I should tell any future doctor or imaging center that I have them.

7. MEDICINES AND PAIN CONTROL
Most oral surgery pain is controlled best by alternating ibuprofen and acetaminophen on a schedule, not by opioids. If an opioid is prescribed
for you, we have discussed the following:
•
It is for short-term use only. New York limits an initial opioid prescription for acute pain to a 7-day supply.
•
Opioids cause drowsiness, constipation, nausea and slowed breathing, and can lead to dependence, addiction and overdose — the danger is
much higher when combined with alcohol, benzodiazepines, muscle relaxants, sleep aids or other sedatives.
•
Do not drive or work while taking them.
•
Keep them locked away from children, teenagers, visitors and pets, and take what you do not use to a drug take-back site. Never share them.
•
Naloxone (Narcan) reverses an overdose, is available without a prescription, and may be recommended for your home.
•
Antibiotics can cause upset stomach, diarrhea, C. difficile infection, yeast infection, rash or a serious allergic reaction, and may make hormonal
birth control less reliable.

8. MY PART IN THE RESULT
•
I have given a complete and accurate medical and dental history, including all conditions, all prescription and non-prescription medicines and
supplements, allergies, recreational drug use and pregnancy, and I will report any change before surgery.
•
I will follow the soft diet I am given — typically nothing hard, crunchy or chewy for the first 8 to 12 weeks. Biting into hard food with a temporary
bridge is the most common cause of early failure.
•
I have been told that smoking and vaping significantly increase the risk that these implants and this bridge will fail, and I have been advised to
stop.

CONSENT FOR A PATIENT-SPECIFIC / SUBPERIOSTEAL IMPLANT
Patient: ______________________________
•
How strong the evidence is. The published studies are small, are mostly case series without a comparison group, and include no randomized
trials. Reviewers have rated the overall certainty of this evidence as very low. Roughly one study in five reports results beyond three years, and
about one in ten beyond five years.
•
What those studies report. In the short and medium term, most of these implants stay in place — reported survival is roughly 70% to 100%,
with an average follow-up of under two years in the largest review. Complications of the gum over the framework are common: part of the
framework becoming exposed through the gum has been reported in about 1 in 4 patients overall, and in some series in as many as 2 out of 3.
Persistent soft-tissue infection was reported in about 1 in 20.
•
What this means for me. My surgeon cannot tell me how long this device will last, cannot promise it will not become exposed or infected,
and cannot rely on long-term studies to predict my result. I am accepting that uncertainty as part of choosing this treatment.
Initial to confirm this was explained to you:
I understand that this is a custom device with limited long-term evidence, that the published studies are small and short, and that
the rate of the gum opening over the framework is substantial.
I understand that no one has told me how many years this device will last, and that no promise or guarantee about its lifespan has
been made to me.
I understand the regulatory status checked in Section 1, including — if it applies to my device — that a custom device is exempt from
the FDA premarket review that mass-produced devices go through.
4. RISKS OF THE SURGERY
Placing this device requires lifting the gum away from the bone over a large area, which makes the surgery longer and the recovery heavier than
for an ordinary implant. No surgery is risk-free, and this list cannot include every possible complication.
•
Common, and usually temporary: significant pain, swelling and bruising of the face and neck, often for a week or more; bleeding and oozing;
stiff jaw and limited opening; sore throat; difficulty eating and speaking for several weeks; numbness of the lip or cheek for hours to days.
•
Less common: infection needing antibiotics, drainage or a second procedure; the wound opening along the incision line; slow healing;
hematoma; damage to the lips, cheeks or tongue; jaw joint pain; scarring; allergic or adverse reaction to a medicine or material, including —
rarely — titanium sensitivity.
•
Uncommon, but serious: nerve injury causing numbness, tingling, burning or pain of the lip, chin, cheek, side of the nose, gums or tongue,
and/or a change in taste. Because the framework is seated over a wide area of bone and may pass close to the mental, inferior alveolar or
infraorbital nerves, this risk is higher than for a single ordinary implant. It usually improves, but it can be permanent; an opening into the
sinus or nose; sinus infection; fracture of a thin, atrophic jaw; infection spreading into the face or neck; heavy bleeding.
•
Rare: medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw (MRONJ), more likely with bone-strengthening or anti-cancer drugs or previous radiation
to the jaws; permanent change in facial appearance; life-threatening complications.
5. RISKS SPECIFIC TO A CUSTOM SUBPERIOSTEAL IMPLANT
•
Framework exposure — the most common problem. The gum over the framework can thin, shrink or open, leaving part of the metal visible or
palpable in the mouth. Sometimes this is stable and simply watched; sometimes it needs a gum graft to cover it; and sometimes it leads to
ongoing infection and to removal of the device.
•

reshaped in the process, healing takes longer, and my options afterwards may be fewer and more difficult than the ones I have today —

recommended at the time of surgery or later, at additional cost.

additional cost. Grinding and clenching increase all of these, and a night guard is usually required.
